jobLines.text: List 3 flights from Boston to Miami with price and departure time

goal:
Do the job below from the input files, then write one JSON file per numbered line.

The input files (label: file):
  - page: input/page.txt

For each numbered job line N, write ONE file output/steps/N.json: a JSON object with exactly these keys.
  "text"  — your answer for that line, as a string.
  "cites" — an object: for each input you drew on, its label as the key and a list of {"claim", "quote"} as the value.
            "claim" is one thing your text relies on; "quote" is words copied EXACTLY from that input (spacing and
            ** or __ marks do not matter). Every number in a claim must also appear in its quote.
  In each claim, copy every number, time and price exactly as the input writes it (for example "9:27 AM", not "09:27"),
  because the check matches the numbers in your claim against your quote.
A job line the brief below marks as a FACTS line is different: its file holds ONLY {"results": [{"quote": "...", "values":
{"<fact>": "<value>"}}]} — one result per thing found, one quote copied exactly from the text of that one result, the values written as the quote
writes them; no "text" and no "cites". A line the brief marks as a TEXT line keeps "text" (free words), and every number in it
must be copied from a quote of an earlier facts line.
Write nothing outside output/, and never edit the files under input/. The file must be complete, valid JSON: a file cut
off before its closing brace counts as not written.

The job, line by line:
1. List 3 flights from Boston to Miami with price and departure time

Job line 1 is a FACTS line. Write output/steps/1.json as {"results": [{"quote": "...", "values": {...}}]} and nothing else — no "text", no "cites".
  One result per thing you find in the input "page": exactly 3 results.
  "quote": ONE quote per result, copied exactly from that result's own text in the input (at most 4000 characters) — never joined from two results.
  "values": one entry per fact below, written exactly as the quote writes it (for example "9:27 AM", not "09:27"; "389", not "389.00").
    - origin city — no value to write; the quote you copy must say "Boston"
    - destination city — no value to write; the quote you copy must say "Miami"
    - price — an amount in US dollars, right after "From"
    - departure time — a time, right after "Departure time:"

The plan the person confirmed: List exactly 3 flights in output/steps/1.json, each with a quoted origin city (Boston), destination city (Miami), a price from the page's "From" label in US dollars, and a departure time from the page's "Departure time:" label.

parts.text: List 3 flights from Boston to Miami with price and departure time

notes: Which 3 flights are listed is not checked: the person did not say how to choose among the page's flights, and choice is not a shape a fact can carry.
Whether the prices and departure times are accurate or current is not checked: that needs a read of the live page, which no stage can do.
Tone and quality of the listing text is not checked: line 1 is a facts line, so its file holds only results and quotes, no prose to judge.
Fact words were copied from the input's own labels rather than the person's words: the price label is "From" (not "from"), and the departure time label is "Departure time:" (not "Leaves").
Money fact uses unit "US dollars" only, as the look gives it; no currency sign was added, because "$" does not show the same amounts as "US dollars" per the look.

Origin and destination facts use the phrase form with a single page word per the look's first listed option ("Boston", "Miami"); the look offered alternatives ("BOS", "Boston Logan International Airport", "MIA", "Miami International Airport") that the schema cannot express as alternatives on one fact.
Count for line 1 is a fact count (min 3, max 3) rather than a minClaims/maxClaims part, because line 1 lists results and so carries one fact part and no claim-count parts.

line 1: "price label" — "US dollars" was listed twice, as a unit and as a currency; it is used once, as the first way to write the price. "$" does not show the same amounts as "US dollars", so it was not used as a second way to write the price. "from" does not show the same values as "From", so it was not used as a second way to read it.
line 1: "departure time label" — "Leaves" does not show the same values as "Departure time:", so it was not used as a second way to read it.
